records.title: Chapter 11 textbook review
records.assignment: Read the summary on printed p. 401. Complete Q2–18 and one of Q22–24 on printed pp. 402–403.
answers: Damage to the right motor cortex most directly affects voluntary movement on the left side because major motor pathways cross; the corpus callosum connects hemispheres but is not the crossing point for all motor fibres.
Match each labelled lobe to evidence: parietal—body sensation and position; occipital—vision; frontal—planning, voluntary movement, and speech production; temporal—hearing and language comprehension.
Sympathetic pathways mobilize energy and cardiovascular/respiratory activity; parasympathetic pathways support recovery and digestion. Their effects vary by organ.
Corpus-callosum surgery can reduce seizure spread between hemispheres, but it does not remove the original seizure focus.
Acetylcholine can depolarize a muscle fibre at a neuromuscular junction; acetylcholinesterase rapidly ends the signal by breaking down acetylcholine.
Poor coordination suggests cerebellar or connected motor-network involvement; a symptom alone cannot locate a lesion with certainty.
A reflex arc is receptor → sensory neuron → CNS integration → motor neuron → effector. Conscious perception can occur after the response begins.
A spinal-cord lesion can interrupt ascending sensory pathways, so signals from below the lesion may not reach the brain even when receptors and peripheral nerves respond.
A complete neuron diagram labels receptor/dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin-forming glia, nodes, terminals, and effector or next cell.
Grey matter is rich in cell bodies, dendrites, synapses, and unmyelinated regions; white matter contains many myelinated axons organized into tracts.
Multiple sclerosis damages CNS myelin and can disrupt communication within the CNS and between the CNS and body; symptoms depend on lesion location.
At rest, potassium is higher inside and sodium higher outside. Selective permeability, potassium leak, trapped anions, and the sodium–potassium pump maintain a negative interior near −70 mV.
Depolarization is driven by sodium entry after threshold; repolarization follows sodium-channel inactivation and potassium efflux. Refractory channel states help keep propagation one-way.
Myelin increases conduction speed because action potentials regenerate mainly at nodes. Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.
An inhibitory transmitter makes threshold less likely by changing membrane conductance; its effect depends on the receptor and ions involved.
Threshold is the membrane voltage needed to trigger a spike. A stronger stimulus does not make one spike larger; it can increase firing frequency and recruit more neurons.
Memory involves distributed networks. The frontal lobe supports working memory and planning, but Alzheimer disease is not confined to one lobe.

Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges. Clinicians may analyze cerebrospinal fluid collected by lumbar puncture for cells, chemistry, culture, or pathogen markers. The meninges do not themselves form the blood–brain barrier; that barrier is created mainly by specialized CNS capillary endothelial cells and supporting structures.

Threshold describes the membrane change needed to trigger an action potential, but pain tolerance cannot be reduced to a single sensory-neuron threshold. Receptor sensitivity, pathway modulation, attention, experience, context, and brain processing all influence pain perception.
For the connection question, botulinum toxin interferes with acetylcholine release, reducing neuromuscular transmission and potentially causing paralysis, including breathing-muscle weakness.

records.title: Chapter 12 textbook review
records.assignment: Read the summary on printed p. 431. Complete Q1–25 and two of Q26–30 on printed pp. 432–433.
answers: Odour molecule → olfactory receptor → receptor potential/action potentials → olfactory bulb and cortex; connections with limbic networks help explain strong emotion and memory associations.
Match receptor to stimulus: photoreceptors—light; mechanoreceptors—pressure, vibration, movement; chemoreceptors—molecules; thermoreceptors—temperature; nociceptors—potential tissue damage.
Rods and cones are retinal photoreceptors. Rods are highly sensitive in dim light; cones support colour and high-acuity vision.
Touch transduction converts skin deformation into an electrical receptor response, then action potentials travel through sensory pathways to the somatosensory cortex.
Phantom-limb sensations can arise because CNS maps and pathways remain active and may reorganize after sensory input from a limb is lost.
Pitch depends on which cochlear regions and hair cells respond; intensity relates to vibration amplitude and neural recruitment. The brain integrates the pattern.
Sensory adaptation reduces response to an unchanging stimulus and helps prioritize changing or significant information.
Pupil light adaptation uses iris muscles: bright light constricts the pupil; dim light dilates it. This is distinct from lens accommodation.
A rod-rich retina supports sensitivity in low light but not sharp colour vision.
The optic-disc blind spot lacks rods and cones. Overlapping visual fields and brain processing usually fill the perceptual gap.
Light changes photoreceptor transmitter release; bipolar and ganglion-cell circuits process the signal, and ganglion axons form the optic nerve.
Visual perception uses occipital and connected cortical networks to combine colour, motion, form, depth, memory, and attention.
Balance integrates visual input, vestibular input from the inner ear, and proprioceptive input from muscles and joints.
For near focus, ciliary contraction reduces zonular tension and the lens becomes rounder; for distance, the lens flattens.
Semicircular canals mainly detect rotational acceleration; utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and head orientation relative to gravity.
Rod dysfunction can impair night and peripheral vision, increasing risk in low-light driving.
The temporal lobe contains important auditory and memory networks, but an injury pattern requires more evidence than one symptom.
Sound pathway: pinna → canal → tympanum → ossicles → oval window → cochlear fluid/membranes → hair cells → auditory nerve → brainstem, thalamus, and auditory cortex.
Repeated loud-sound exposure can damage cochlear hair-cell stereocilia in frequency-specific regions. This activity never uses browser tones as a hearing test.
Sensory deprivation can disrupt orientation, mood, and thought because sensory input supports awareness of body and environment; effects depend on duration and context.
A protective helmet design should reduce impact to the whole skull, including the occipital region; it should not be described as protecting only one lobe.
Colour-vision supports should account for cone-photopigment differences and should never rely on colour as the only information channel.
Glasses and hearing aids compensate for particular barriers; implants have different indications, benefits, limits, risks, and access requirements.
Age-related loss of lens flexibility reduces accommodation for near objects; converging lenses can compensate for presbyopia.
Dogs have more olfactory receptor tissue and extensive olfactory processing, supporting much greater odour sensitivity than humans.
Afterimages reflect temporary adaptation in cone pathways; staring at an intense source is unsafe and unnecessary.
Dogs have dichromatic colour vision. They distinguish blue and yellow ranges better than red–green differences, so colour should not be the only cue in a working-dog signal.

A stronger sensory stimulus can recruit more receptors and increase action-potential frequency, but pain perception also depends on spinal and brain processing. Individual pain tolerance is not a direct measure of one receptor threshold.

The infant-odour observation supports a testable association, not a proven mechanism or treatment. A sound investigation would compare breathing outcomes under controlled conditions, account for confounders, and use clinical safety oversight.
Neurotoxins can block receptors, alter transmitter release, or change breakdown. Their medical potential depends on targeted dose, delivery, benefit, and risk.
correctionNotes: The assignment corrects the overlapping source wording ‘two from 25–30’ to ‘two of Q26–30’.

records.title: Chapter 13 textbook review
records.assignment: Read the summary on printed p. 463. Complete Q2, Q6, Q10, Q12–19, Q23–25, and one of Q26–30 on printed pp. 464–465.
answers: The pituitary releases several tropic hormones, but the hypothalamus regulates anterior-pituitary output. The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic neurons.
Cortisol, epinephrine, glucagon, and hGH can support increased blood glucose through different mechanisms; insulin generally supports a decrease. Timing and tissue matter.
Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic in a simplified glucose model: insulin supports uptake/storage and reduced liver output; glucagon supports liver glucose release.
A startle activates sympathetic pathways and the adrenal medulla rapidly; hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal signalling and cortisol develop over a longer interval.
Norepinephrine can be a neurotransmitter released from sympathetic neurons or a hormone released by the adrenal medulla; route and target distinguish the role.
Aldosterone increases kidney sodium reabsorption and influences water retention, blood volume, and pressure. It does not directly add water to blood.

Historical source terminology for congenital hypothyroidism is outdated. Use congenital hypothyroidism and explain that early diagnosis and thyroid-hormone treatment protect growth and neurodevelopment.
Loss of anterior-pituitary output can reduce hGH, TSH, ACTH, gonadotropins, and prolactin, producing multiple downstream hormone patterns.
Low thyroxine with high TSH suggests a thyroid-level limitation; low thyroxine with low or inappropriately normal TSH suggests reduced central drive. Neither pattern proves one cause alone.
A hot-day activity response integrates sweating and skin blood-flow control, thirst, ADH-mediated water conservation, and aldosterone-linked sodium regulation.
Short-term stress emphasizes sympathetic/adrenal-medulla signalling; sustained stress recruits cortisol and other systems. Benefits and costs depend on duration and context.

An overcrowding investigation could compare clearly defined populations and measure relevant stress indicators, but age, health, income, environment, work, sleep, and other confounders prevent a simple causal conclusion. Ethical, non-diagnostic methods and informed consent are required.
If exercise lowers glucose, adding insulin without clinical guidance could lower it further. Personal treatment decisions require an individual plan, not a textbook rule.
For the ACTH loop: hypothalamus → CRH → anterior pituitary → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol, with cortisol feedback to hypothalamus and pituitary.
Steroid hormones are synthesized from cholesterol. A balanced diet supplies essential nutrients, but eating more lipid does not directly increase a desired hormone.
Performance-enhancing hGH claims require evidence of benefit, harms, fairness, legality, dose, and long-term outcomes.
Animal research decisions require scientific necessity, welfare safeguards, alternatives, and ethical oversight; historical benefit does not settle every current case.

Type 2 diabetes risk is multifactorial. Population patterns can involve genetics, age, social determinants, access to care, food environments, sleep, medications, activity, and other factors; avoid blaming individuals or treating one association as a complete cause.

For a glucose-time graph, identify the meal-related rise, compare peak and recovery patterns, and connect the pattern to insulin and glucagon without diagnosing a person. Exercise can change glucose use, so treatment decisions must remain individualized and clinical.

records.title: Unit A — Textbook Unit 5 Review
records.context: The textbook calls this material Unit 5; in this course it is Unit A.
records.assignment: Complete Q1–51 on printed pp. 468–471, then compare your reasoning with the answer guide.
answers: Label a neuron with dendrites, cell body, axon, terminals, and membrane transport proteins.
Corrected: Schwann cells form PNS myelin; oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin. Myelin supports saltatory conduction.
Sensory input travels toward the CNS, interneurons integrate, motor output travels to effectors; a withdrawal reflex can precede conscious pain.
Coordination evidence points toward cerebellar or connected motor networks, but does not prove one lesion.
An action-potential graph should show rest, threshold, depolarization, repolarization, undershoot, and recovery.
CNS = brain and spinal cord; PNS = nerves. Somatic and autonomic pathways have different effectors and control patterns.
Choose any three senses and connect receptor type, pathway, brain region, and resulting perception.
Mechanoreceptors respond to deformation; photoreceptors to light; chemoreceptors to molecules; thermoreceptors to temperature.
Trace light through cornea, aqueous humour, pupil, lens, vitreous humour, and retina; retinal ganglion axons form the optic nerve.
Semicircular canals detect rotation; utricle/saccule detect linear acceleration and head orientation.
Outer/middle ear transmit vibration; cochlear hair cells transduce mechanical energy into neural signals.
Light changes photoreceptor transmitter release; retinal circuits and the optic nerve carry processed information onward.
Aqueous humour supports the cornea/anterior eye; vitreous humour supports the globe and retina.
Bright light constricts the pupil; dim light dilates it. Accommodation changes lens shape, not pupil size.
Neurotransmitters act across local synapses; hormones travel in blood. Both require receptors and can use feedback.
Sympathetic and parasympathetic effects are organ-specific and often opposing, not universal on/off states.
Driving emphasizes fast sensory-motor control; fasting glucose emphasizes endocrine control; exercise integrates both.
Heat and activity recruit thirst, ADH, skin blood-flow/sweating responses, and sodium-regulation pathways.
Rapid stress uses sympathetic/adrenal-medulla pathways; slower support includes cortisol and other endocrine responses.
Low iodine can reduce thyroid-hormone synthesis, increase TSH drive, and contribute to goitre; other causes require evidence.
Endocrine research is difficult because concentrations are low, release is variable, glands produce multiple hormones, and systems compensate.
Only cells with compatible receptors and response machinery respond to a circulating hormone.
Sympathetic neurons and adrenal-medulla hormones coordinate the rapid fight-or-flight response.
Corrected: type 1 diabetes involves autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, not alpha cells. Insulin treatment requires an individual clinical plan.
The hypothalamus controls anterior-pituitary secretion and produces hormones released from the posterior pituitary; evaluate the ‘master gland’ label critically.
Low ADH signalling can produce large volumes of dilute urine and intense thirst; classroom evidence is not diagnostic.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and hGH can raise or support glucose availability by different routes.
TRH → TSH → thyroid hormone, with thyroid hormone feeding back to hypothalamus and pituitary.
Adrenal cortex: cortisol, aldosterone, and sex steroids; each has different targets and control.
Organize each pathway as stimulus/control → gland → hormone → target → response → feedback evidence.
Endurance-stress evidence may include heat strain, dehydration, glucose disruption, reduced gut blood flow, and sodium imbalance; conclusions require measured data.
Excess hGH before growth plates close can cause excessive linear growth; after closure it produces a different tissue-growth pattern.
A nervous-system map should include receptors, CNS, PNS, sensory routes, motor routes, and the muscles used to read and respond.
Withdrawal: nociceptor → sensory neuron → spinal interneuron → motor neuron → muscle; ascending pathways support later conscious pain.
Match evidence cautiously: auditory—temporal networks; visual—occipital; body sensation—parietal; voluntary movement—frontal. Smell involves olfactory/limbic networks, not simply parietal cortex.

Corrected: increasing extracellular potassium generally depolarizes a neuron by reducing the potassium gradient; changing extracellular sodium affects spike driving force. Direction depends on ion gradients and permeability.
At rest, sodium is high outside and potassium high inside. Sodium entry depolarizes; potassium efflux repolarizes; refractory channel states support recovery.
Botulinum toxin reduces acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions, weakening targeted muscle contraction; it is a potent toxin with controlled medical uses.
Dense cone packing supports high visual acuity in the foveal region; acuity also depends on optics and neural organization.
A neuron’s spike is all-or-none, but frequency threshold and receptor tuning differ. Stronger stimuli can recruit more cells and increase firing rate.
Excess water lowers plasma osmotic concentration, suppressing ADH and increasing water excretion; severe hyponatremia is a medical emergency, not a classroom experiment.
After a meal, insulin should rise; when glucose falls between meals or during activity, glucagon supports liver glucose output.
Repeated samples at controlled times and averaging reduce random variation; trends still cannot diagnose a person without clinical criteria and context.
Myopia focuses distant images in front of the retina and is commonly corrected with a diverging lens.
Frequency-specific cochlear hair-cell damage can produce a notch or region of elevated thresholds; cause needs more evidence than one audiogram.
Developing frontal networks support planning and motor learning, but PET activity reflects task-related metabolism, not a simple measure of intelligence.
Brain research can support diagnosis and treatment while raising privacy, access, and discrimination concerns.
MS damages CNS myelin; Alzheimer disease affects progressive brain networks; prion disease has a different protein-based mechanism. Do not collapse them into one disorder.
Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake and prolongs synaptic dopamine signalling; addiction involves distributed learning, reward, stress, and control systems.
Long-duration stress can alter metabolism, pressure, immune activity, sleep, and cognition. Stress reduction and care are contextual, not a one-drug solution.
Hypothyroid symptoms plus low iodine intake suggest a testable hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Measure thyroid hormones/TSH and seek clinical evaluation.
correctionNotes: The source key title says pp. 466–469, but the actual Unit 5 review occupies printed pp. 468–471.
